opus-5.5.text:
I think it came from a pretty practical frustration. When I was doing RL research as a student, I noticed that a huge amount of my time wasn't going into ideas. It was going into fighting the tooling: reimplementing baselines, debugging environment wrappers, waiting for slow rollouts, and trying to figure out whether a result was real or just a bug or a random seed. And I realized I wasn't the only one. Basically everyone in the field was rebuilding the same wheels, often slightly broken in different ways, which made results hard to compare and hard to trust.

So at some point I asked myself: where can I actually have more leverage? If I write one more paper with a small algorithmic tweak, maybe it helps a little. But if I build a framework or a fast environment engine that thousands of people use, then every one of those researchers iterates faster and more reliably. That multiplier felt much bigger to me. That was the motivation behind things like Tianshou, and later working on speeding up environment execution. In RL, the bottleneck is very often the system, not the algorithm.

I also just enjoy engineering. There's a very satisfying feedback loop when you make something ten times faster or cleaner, and you can measure it immediately. Research can be much more ambiguous.

And honestly, I came to believe the line between research and infrastructure is kind of artificial. A lot of the big progress in RL and in large models has come from scaling and from people who could make the system work at a size nobody else could. Good infrastructure *is* research capability. So I don't think of it as leaving research. It's more like working on the part of the stack that I think determines how fast research can move.

r001.rationale: The response says building a framework or faster environment engine would help many researchers iterate faster and more reliably, framing the move into infrastructure as facilitating others’ RL research.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a single dramatic decision. It came out of frustration, really.

When I was doing RL research, I kept running into the same problem over and over. I'd have an idea for an algorithm, and then I'd spend eighty percent of my time not on the idea, but on getting the experiment to run at all. The environment was slow, the data pipeline was a mess, the results weren't reproducible between my machine and a teammate's machine. And then you'd see a paper claim a big improvement, you'd try to reproduce it, and you couldn't tell if the gap was the algorithm or some implementation detail nobody wrote down.

That bothered me. RL is already a field where the signal is noisy. If the tooling adds more noise on top, you can't really learn anything from your experiments.

So I started building things to fix my own problems. Tianshou came out of that. I wanted a codebase where the algorithms were written cleanly enough that you could actually read them and trust them, and modular enough that swapping one component didn't break everything else. Later with EnvPool, it was the same instinct but on the environment side. If simulation is the bottleneck, and in RL it very often is, then making environments run an order of magnitude faster changes what research is even possible. You can run more seeds, bigger sweeps, and actually get statistically meaningful answers.

What I realized along the way is that infrastructure has this leverage effect. One good algorithm paper helps the people who read it. One good library helps everyone who uses it, including people working on ideas I would never have thought of. For me that felt like a bigger contribution than one more incremental algorithm.

And I'll admit, I just enjoy it. I like the engineering. I like when something that used to take a day runs in ten minutes. That satisfaction is very concrete in a way research results sometimes aren't.

r001.rationale: The candidate says infrastructure removes research bottlenecks and that a good library helps everyone who uses it, enabling research beyond his own ideas.

astra-6.text:
I started to see infrastructure as a bottleneck to doing good RL research. You can have an interesting algorithmic idea, but testing it means getting a whole loop working: generating experience, training, evaluating, and understanding what went wrong. If that loop is slow or unreliable, it limits how much you can learn.

So for me, building infrastructure is a way to enable research. Better infrastructure makes experiments faster and results easier to trust. Instead of improving one algorithm, you can help people explore many more ideas. That’s what made the shift compelling to me.

r001.rationale: The candidate says infrastructure is “a way to enable research” and helps people explore more ideas, framing the shift as facilitating others’ RL research.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it was realizing that the bottleneck wasn’t always the algorithm. In RL, you spend a lot of time getting the whole loop to work: generating experience, running training, evaluating the policy, and figuring out why something broke. If that loop is slow or unreliable, it really limits the research you can do.

I became interested in making that loop better. Building infrastructure felt like a way to help more people experiment faster, instead of solving those same engineering problems over and over. So I see it as a continuation of my interest in RL—working on the foundation that makes the research possible.

r001.rationale: She describes infrastructure as helping more people experiment faster and providing the foundation that makes RL research possible.
